findings.summary: Fuzzing is an automated software testing technique that feeds invalid, unexpected, or random inputs to a program to provoke crashes, assertion failures, or memory leaks. It targets programs that process structured inputs like file formats or protocols, generating semi-valid inputs that bypass initial parsers but expose hidden corner cases. The method traces back to 1950s punched-card testing and was formalized in 1988 by Prof. Barton Miller's graduate class, which crashed 25-33% of tested UNIX utilities. Modern variants include mutation-based fuzzers that modify seed corpora and generation-based fuzzers that synthesize inputs from models. The technique became prominent in security after high-profile discoveries such as Shellshock and Heartbleed, and is now offered as cloud services like Google's ClusterFuzz and Microsoft's Project Springfield.

mechanisms.title: Mutation-based fuzzing
mechanisms.explanation: A mutation-based fuzzer modifies an existing corpus of seed inputs to generate semi-valid variants. For example, when fuzzing an image library, valid PNG files serve as seeds that are mutated to produce variants likely to trigger deeper program behaviors and corner cases.

mechanisms.title: Generation-based fuzzing
mechanisms.explanation: A generation-based fuzzer creates inputs from scratch using a provided input model, without relying on a pre-existing seed corpus. Some fuzzers combine both approaches to generate and mutate inputs.
